claims.text: The baseline system consists of an elemental Cr coating deposited directly on a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate.
A TiN layer approximately 20–100 nm thick should be deposited between the Cr coating and the Zr-alloy substrate.
The deposited TiN barrier will be continuous and dense.
The TiN barrier will remain thermally stable under the stated exposure conditions.
TiN has sufficiently low atomic diffusivity to act as a diffusion barrier at the Cr/Zr-alloy interface.
The TiN layer forms an inert interface between the Cr coating and the Zr-alloy substrate.
The TiN barrier reduces atomic mobility at the Cr–Zr interface at elevated temperature.
Reduced interfacial atomic mobility inhibits Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
Inhibiting Cr–Zr interdiffusion prevents the formation of deleterious intermetallic phases under accident conditions.
Cr–Zr intermetallic phases promote coating degradation under accident conditions.
The TiN layer does not interfere with the protective oxidation behavior of the Cr coating in normal subcritical-water operation.
Relative to directly Cr-coated cladding, the TiN-modified system will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
Relative to directly Cr-coated cladding, the TiN-modified system will retain better coating integrity during high-temperature steam events.
The TiN-modified system will provide corrosion protection in subcritical water similar to that of the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
Directly applied elemental Cr coatings undergo premature failure because of Cr–Zr interdiffusion in accident-relevant high-temperature steam.
The proposed barrier is expected to be beneficial in subcritical-water operation at approximately 350–400°C over extended durations.
The proposed barrier is expected to be beneficial in steam at temperatures up to approximately 1200°C for exposures lasting minutes to 1–2 hours.
